sentences.text: Gryposaurus was a large herbivore capable of walking on two or four legs, reaching lengths of about 8 meters.
The type specimen of Gryposaurus notabilis represents an animal approximately 8.2 meters long.
Skin impressions reveal that this dinosaur had scutes up to 3.8 centimeters long on its flanks and tail.
Gregory S. Paul estimated Gryposaurus latidens to be 7.5 meters long and 2.5 metric tons in mass.
He also estimated Gryposaurus notabilis and G. monumentensis to be 8 meters long and 3 metric tons in mass.
Gryposaurus is based on specimen NMC 2278, found in 1913 by George F. Sternberg in the Dinosaur Park Formation along the Red Deer River.
This specimen was described by Lawrence Lambe, who was particularly interested in the nasal arch.
Further research revealed a second species, G. latidens, found in slightly older rocks in Montana compared to the classic Alberta localities.
New material from the Kaiparowits Formation in Utah represents the species G. monumentensis.
Gryposaurus had skull joints allowing a grinding motion and dental batteries containing hundreds of teeth, with only a few in use at once.
Evidence suggests Gryposaurus was both a grazer and a browser, feeding on tough, fibrous plant material.
G. latidens has a nasal arch farther forward on the snout than G. notabilis and teeth that reflect iguanodont-like characteristics.

It is believed the nasal arch held a skin sac that could be inflated to make a sound for social communication, and it is speculated that males raised skin coloration during mating season to increase blood flow.
The type species of Gryposaurus is G. notabilis.
As of 2016, three species are recognized as valid: G. notabilis, G. latidens, and G. monumentensis, while G. alsatei remains questionable.
The informal name "Hadrosauravus" was an early, unused name for G. latidens.
Current research suggests that Hadrosaurus can be distinguished from Gryposaurus based on differences in the upper arm and ilium.
Gryposaurus lived in North America during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 80 to 75 million years ago, though it lived between 85 and 66 million years ago.
A possible species from the Javelina Formation in Texas might extend the genus's temporal range to 66 million years ago.
Gryposaurus may have preferred riverine habitats.
William Parks named a skeleton from the Dinosaur Park Formation as Kritosaurus incurvimanus rather than Gryposaurus incurvimanus, reflecting the debate over whether the two genera were synonymous.
